title: Immigration Is Not a Fringe Issue
author: Greisa Martínez Rosas
body:
At a Senate forum on ICE violence, I listened to the sons of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo describe the morning their father was shot dead by ICE agents while on his way to work. Besides them sat and wept the families of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti.

Next to me were clergy wearing t-shirts that said “Connected Americans” and whispering prayers as they listened to the testimony of families whose loved ones had been killed in the streets. While a number of elected officials sat in the front of the room, they were not the center. The families and those of us there to bear witness were.

The demands made that day by people like Lorenzo’s sons were not unfamiliar to me. They’re the demands I hear from people every day: swift justice that remedies what our communities have been forced to endure and a future where all working people can live with safety, stability, and dignity. It takes courage to speak out when your voice breaks. These families did it anyway.

Meanwhile, throughout the midterms, Democratic candidates were advised by centrist think tanks and commentators to talk less about immigration and more about the economy. As if one were a political liability and the other a path back to working families. No one in that Senate room was living a separate problem.

The failure of both Democrats and Republicans to deliver a path to citizenship has pushed economic security further out of reach for working people, leaving millions of workers vulnerable to deportation, family separation, and a future defined by instability and uncertainty. Multiply that across every workplace where someone has been killed, detained, deported, or stripped of their ability to work, and the consequences are anything but abstract. They affect us all. Immigrants sustain the industries, workplaces, and communities we all depend on. And those who insist we must choose between a path to citizenship or supporting working families have yet to stand with the families bearing the cost of that false choice.

The midterm results should make it impossible to ignore the truth: there is no such thing as a functioning economy for working people without immigrants. Voters rejected an administration whose immigration policies have made life more expensive and less secure for working families. Even the President admitted what those families already knew. In an interview with 60 Minutes, Donald Trump said that his mass deportations “might have been too tough,” costing both him and Republicans control of Congress. “I get hurt because we also took people who had good jobs.”

Soon after the episode aired, Trump named Stephen Miller, the central architect of the deadly raids, family separations, and mass deportations, as his next White House Chief of Staff. A president who acknowledges the cost of mass deportations went on to promote the man who built it. This is a warning to every member of the incoming Congress, newly elected and returning: the election did not end this fight. It's likely they will escalate it. We will be organizing so that Members of Congress defend the people they were elected to represent.

What Americans are up against is formidable. The numbers describe the mass deportation machinery Congress has helped fund. ICE's detention population grew by more than 70% between January 2025 and April 2026. Congress still approved approximately $75 billion in additional ICE funding, including $45 billion for immigration detention, despite polling showing that 58% of Americans believe ICE's enforcement actions have gone too far. And in the last two years, 60 people have died in immigration enforcement custody or encounters, according to The Guardian.

The harm does not stop with immigrants. An investigation by ProPublica revealed that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been caught up in immigration enforcement practices. Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti amongst them. Our broken, violent immigration system impacts neighborhoods, workplaces, and families across the country. No one is left out of its reach. And our economy suffers when the millions of working people whose labor helps sustain it are left vulnerable without a path to citizenship.

My home state of Texas shows what it looks like when a candidate refuses to treat immigration, human rights, and the economy as separate issues. Salgado Araujo lived and worked in Texas for 35 years, putting his three sons through college as a proud, hardworking father. As James Talarico campaigned for his Senate seat, he spoke of his death and committed to ICE accountability and citizenship. Four months to the day after the shooting, the now senator-elect visited Salgado’s memorial in Houston, pledging to seek justice and adding his “I voted” sticker, alongside many other fellow Texans, to the memorial site where Salgado Araujo was shot and killed.

The sticker can be seen as a promise; an oath to use every tool available to protect communities against the terror that has stolen the lives of fathers, mothers, workers, and loved ones across our communities. The organizers, voters, community leaders, and ordinary Americans who made it possible for Talarico to win are now watching whether he and other newly-elected Members of Congress will honor that oath in January.

Strongly worded letters, congressional investigations, and modest cuts to immigration enforcement funding will not be enough in this new Congress. Democrats must pursue a fundamental change in direction, starting with a pathway to citizenship and ensuring immigrants are protected in every legislative priority the new Congress advances.

Voters want leaders willing to confront an enforcement agenda that is tearing families apart, destabilizing workplaces, and wasting billions of their taxpayer dollars, while they’re left struggling simply to make ends meet. And they want leaders who understand that protecting immigrant workers is essential to building an economy that works for everyone.

Electoral wins alone will not protect the millions of people—both citizens and immigrants—whose livelihoods and futures remain at risk. We cannot afford another Congress that recognizes the issue but fails to deliver a solution.

Voters, especially Black, Latino, young, and working-class people, have done their part by rejecting Trump’s agenda at the ballot box. Now Democrats must do theirs. With Stephen Miller's ability to escalate the administration's cruelty, the incoming Congress cannot settle for symbolic resistance or half measures. A pathway to citizenship is the floor of what Congress must deliver. Millions of working people will be organizing to make it so, because the people we love belong here for good.
